clinicalPearls: A rare, slow-growing glioneuronal tumour (CNS WHO grade 1) of young adults, arising characteristically in the posterior fossa around the fourth ventricle
The midline, periventricular location commonly causes headache, ataxia and, when the fourth ventricle is obstructed, hydrocephalus
MRI typically shows a well-circumscribed, partly cystic lesion with variable enhancement near the fourth ventricle, aqueduct or pineal region
Histology shows a biphasic pattern: neurocytic rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes together with a pilocytic astrocytoma-like glial component
FGFR1 alterations, sometimes with PIK3CA or NF1 changes, are recurrent molecular features
The neurocytic rosettes are synaptophysin-positive, confirming neuronal differentiation
Behaviour is indolent, and surgery is the mainstay, though location often limits complete resection
reference.pathophysiology: Rosette-forming glioneuronal tumour is a rare, low-grade neoplasm with both neuronal and glial differentiation, arising most often in the midline posterior fossa around the fourth ventricle and adjacent structures, and sometimes in the pineal region or aqueduct. It is characterised by a biphasic architecture: a neurocytic component forming neurocytic rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes, and a glial component resembling pilocytic astrocytoma. The neurocytic elements express synaptophysin, confirming neuronal differentiation. Recurrent molecular alterations, particularly of the FGFR1 gene and sometimes PIK3CA and NF1, drive its development. Growth is slow, and clinical features arise mainly from its periventricular location and obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow rather than from aggressive behaviour.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the fourth-ventricular/periventricular mass
Assessment of ventricular size for obstructive hydrocephalus
Histopathology demonstrating neurocytic rosettes and a pilocytic-like glial component
Synaptophysin immunohistochemistry to confirm neuronal differentiation
FGFR1 (and where indicated PIK3CA/NF1) molecular testing
Craniospinal MRI where dissemination is a concern
redFlags: Obstructive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure
Progressive brainstem or cerebellar signs from a fourth-ventricular mass
Postoperative neurological deficits given the eloquent location
Unexpectedly rapid growth suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable given the indolent, grade 1 nature of the tumour, and gross total resection can be curative. However, its midline posterior fossa location adjacent to the brainstem and cerebellar structures often limits complete removal and carries a risk of surgical morbidity, so residual tumour may be monitored or, uncommonly, treated further.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for pilocytic astrocytoma or ependymoma and misjudging prognosis or adjuvant therapy
Pursuing aggressive resection in an eloquent location and causing avoidable deficits
Not confirming neuronal differentiation with synaptophysin staining
Failing to recognise and relieve obstructive hydrocephalus
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: Maximal safe surgical resection is the primary treatment; gross total resection can be curative given the grade 1 biology.

Extent of resection is balanced against the risk of neurological injury given the eloquent midline posterior fossa location; subtotal resection is accepted when further dissection risks brainstem or cerebellar damage.
Obstructive hydrocephalus from fourth ventricular involvement is treated directly, typically with endoscopic third ventriculostomy or ventriculoperitoneal shunting, before or during resection.
Asymptomatic residual tumour after subtotal resection is generally observed with surveillance imaging rather than treated immediately.
Adjuvant radiotherapy is reserved for disease that is progressive, recurrent, or symptomatic and not manageable surgically; it is not routine first-line treatment.
Repeat resection is considered for recurrent or progressive disease when technically feasible and likely to relieve symptoms or mass effect.
Radiotherapy is the next line considered when recurrence or progression is not amenable to further resection.

FGFR-targeted therapy has been proposed for progressive or unresectable disease in individual cases given recurrent FGFR1 alterations (sometimes with PIK3CA or NF1 changes), but it is not established first-line systemic therapy.
There is no established role for conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy in this tumour and none should be inferred.
Serial surveillance brain MRI is used to detect residual tumour growth or recurrence after initial surgery.
Ventricular size is monitored postoperatively and at follow-up to detect recurrent obstructive hydrocephalus.
Unexpectedly rapid growth on surveillance imaging should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, as this would be atypical for a grade 1 tumour.
Management should occur within a neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team from diagnosis given the resection-versus-morbidity tradeoff.

Referral to a centre with FGFR-targeted therapy experience or a relevant clinical trial should be considered for progressive or unresectable disease that has exhausted standard surgical and radiotherapy options.
